headline: South Florida Hit by Compound Flooding as King Tides and Heavy Rainfall Converge — While Hurricane Rachel Organizes in the Eastern Pacific
overview: As September closes out, an unusually active natural events period continues across multiple continents. South Florida is being struck today by a dual threat of king tides and intense rainfall — up to 86.8mm recorded in Miami — compounding ongoing coastal flooding. In the eastern Pacific, the El Niño-fueled 2026 hurricane season has produced yet another threat as Tropical Storm Rachel intensified into hurricane strength by late September, and Anak Krakatau in Indonesia continues its prolonged eruption cycle, now visibly reshaping the Sunda Strait island.

events.title: South Florida Compound Flooding — King Tides and Heavy Rain Converge on Miami, Fort Lauderdale
events.summary: South Florida is experiencing severe compound flooding today as peak king tides coincide with heavy rainfall, with Miami recording approximately 86.8mm of precipitation — among the highest totals of any major city globally today. CBS Miami reported the flooding threat as active this morning (September 30), with coastal roads inundated in Miami, Fort Lauderdale, and surrounding areas. The combination of sea-level-rise-amplified king tides and stalled tropical moisture is making this one of the most significant flooding days for the region in recent weeks, and is a distinct escalation beyond the Florida Keys inundation event reported on September 29.

events.title: Hurricane Rachel Intensifies in Eastern Pacific — El Niño Season's Latest Threat
events.location: Eastern North Pacific Ocean (off Mexico's Pacific Coast)
events.summary: Tropical Storm Rachel, the 17th named storm of the hyperactive 2026 Eastern Pacific season, was forecast to intensify into a hurricane by Tuesday, September 29, as it tracked west-northwestward away from Mexico's coast. The storm is part of a remarkable El Niño-driven Pacific season that has already produced the record-setting Category 5 Hurricane Polo just days prior. While Rachel is currently expected to remain offshore and not make landfall, it continues to generate large swells and is being closely monitored by the National Hurricane Center.

articles.title: Tropical Storm Rachel Intensifying Off Mexico's Pacific Coast, Forecast to Become a Hurricane Tuesday

events.title: M4.2 Earthquake Rattles Puget Sound — Over 9,000 Reports of Shaking Across Seattle Metro
events.location: Wauna (near Gig Harbor / Port Orchard), Washington, USA
events.summary: A magnitude 4.2 earthquake struck approximately 6 km west-northwest of Wauna, Washington on Tuesday evening (September 29, 21:05 UTC), with shaking felt across a remarkably wide area including Seattle, Tacoma, Bremerton, Olympia, and Issaquah. Over 9,011 felt reports were submitted to USGS — an exceptionally high count for a sub-M5.0 event, reflecting both the dense population of the Puget Sound region and the quake's shallow depth of roughly 28 km. No tsunami alert was issued and the USGS assigned a green alert level, but the event underscores the seismic hazard facing one of the Pacific Northwest's most populated corridors.

events.title: M6.6 Earthquake Strikes Loyalty Islands, New Caledonia — Shallow and Widely Felt
events.summary: A strong magnitude 6.6 earthquake struck 80 km east-northeast of Tadine, New Caledonia on September 25 at 21:23 UTC, at a very shallow depth of just 10 km, making it capable of generating intense local shaking. USGS assigned a green alert level and no tsunami alert was issued, though the shallow depth and proximity to island communities warranted close monitoring. The event was confirmed by both USGS and The Watchers reporting network, with 11 felt reports submitted despite the region's sparse population.

events.title: Anak Krakatau Eruption Reshapes Sunda Strait — New Landmass Emerges, Nearby Island Vegetation Scorched
events.summary: Anak Krakatau's prolonged 2026 eruption cycle — elevated to Level III Alert status since July — has now produced measurable and lasting environmental changes, marking a significant escalation beyond the 50,000-foot ash blast reported on September 28. A new landmass has emerged near the volcanic island, possibly representing a new eruption center, while satellite data shows that ash drift has caused the vegetation index on neighboring Sertung Island to collapse from 0.72 to near zero, indicating widespread vegetation kill. The volcano erupted continuously for 25 hours between September 4–6 alone, and activity has remained intense through the end of September.

events.title: Spain's Largest Wildfire of 2026 Burns 460 Hectares in Galicia — Stabilized After Major Air and Ground Response
events.location: Calvos de Randín, Ourense, Galicia, Spain
events.summary: A major wildfire ignited in the parish of Randín, Galicia on September 25, rapidly expanding to approximately 460 hectares by the following day — making it the largest single wildfire recorded in Spain during 2026. The blaze burned through steep terrain in the Ourense province, challenging firefighting crews before being stabilized near midnight between Friday and Saturday (September 25–26), according to Galicia Press. Reuters Connect reported aerial and ground crews battling the fire across difficult hillside terrain; no civilian casualties were confirmed in available reporting.

events.title: Polo Remnant Moisture Continues Widespread Flooding Across a Dozen US States
events.location: Desert Southwest to Great Plains, USA
events.summary: The moisture plume from the remnants of Hurricane Polo continues to fuel flooding across an expansive area of the United States stretching from Arizona and New Mexico northward through Utah, Colorado, Texas, Kansas, Nebraska, and Iowa, with heavy rainfall totals still being reported across multiple states. The event has now persisted for multiple days, and weather data shows ongoing precipitation across the central US corridor as the moisture continues to interact with mid-latitude weather systems. With the 2026 wildfire season already having burned more than 8.5 million acres nationally, the flooding rains — while destructive — are simultaneously offering some relief to drought- and fire-stressed landscapes across the southwest.
